For injector faults, have injectors flow-tested and replaced individually as needed and use quality fuel with periodic injector-cleaning additives. Diagnose with a Mercedes-capable scan tool before parts replacement.

rows.howToFix: Have the timing chain, tensioner, and guide rails inspected if a rattle develops; replacement of the chain and tensioner before it jumps avoids far costlier internal engine damage. Chain replacement is labour-intensive (front cover access), so addressing it early is essential. Use correct-spec low-SAPS diesel oil and keep service intervals tight, as oil condition affects chain and tensioner wear.

rows.howToFix: Diagnosis requires scanning the roof control system, checking switch status, verifying trunk separator position, and inspecting hydraulic cylinders and lines for fluid leaks. Repairs range from microswitch or latch adjustment to replacement of roof cylinders or pump components; typical costs run $300-$800 for sensor/latch fixes and $1,500-$4,000 for hydraulic repairs. Fluid contamination or low hydraulic level should also be corrected to prevent repeat failures.

rows.title: Rear Subframe Corrosion and Cracking
rows.howToFix: Inspect the rear subframe on a lift, especially around control arm and differential mounting areas, and check for flaking rust, perforation, or cracks. Minor corrosion may be treated temporarily, but advanced rust requires rear subframe replacement and transfer of suspension components; total repair commonly runs $2,500-$5,500 depending on hardware, bushings, and labor. Alignment is required after repair, and heavily corroded fasteners often add labor time.

Verify power-steering fluid level/condition first, as low or contaminated fluid can mimic the fault.

rows.title: Thermostat / Coolant Pump Housing Leaks
rows.howToFix: Pressure-test the cooling system, inspect the thermostat housing and pump area for dried coolant residue, and verify there are no leaks from hoses or expansion tank connections. Typical repair involves replacing the thermostat housing, seals, and sometimes the water pump; most jobs fall between $500 and $1,400 depending on parts replaced and labor access. Coolant should be refilled with the correct Mercedes-spec fluid and the system properly bled.

Most independent shops charge about $180-$450 depending on labor access and part quality.

Repair may involve cleaning and drying connectors, repairing corroded wiring, resealing leak points, or replacing the SAM module if internal damage is severe. Typical costs range from $250 for minor wiring cleanup to $1,500 for module replacement and programming.

A full replacement PSE unit is the durable fix if the board is too far gone. Fixing the underlying boot water leak prevents recurrence.

rows.title: Water Leaks into Trunk and Spare-Wheel Well from Blocked Drains / Boot Seals
rows.howToFix: Clear the boot/roof drain tubes and the spare-well drain, and re-seat or replace the boot seal. Owners diagnose the entry point by drying the boot and pouring water over the rear of the car to find the ingress point. Catching it early keeps repairs cheap; ignoring it risks a corroded PSE pump and a rusted spare well.

rows.title: M271 Camshaft Adjuster (VVT) Magnet Solenoid Failure and Oil Intrusion
rows.howToFix: Replace the camshaft adjuster magnet solenoids and fit Mercedes' updated oil-stop connector/harness (Oelstoppkabel, e.g. A2711502733) that resists oil migration; clean oil from the connector and harness. Because the adjuster still tends to seep, periodic replacement (roughly every 30,000-40,000 miles) is common, and more frequent oil changes slow sludge buildup. A quick diagnostic is swapping intake/exhaust magnets to see if the fault code follows the part.

A neglected fluid service accelerates the failure, so periodic 722.9 fluid changes are recommended.

If the injector has seized, a dedicated injector puller (or in severe cases head removal) is needed. Failed/leaking injectors should be replaced with revised parts. Preventive washer replacement around 100,000 km is recommended.
